claims.text: Adding SiC as a secondary phase to ZrB2 enables densification at sintering temperatures below 1700 °C.
The SiC addition produces a composite microstructure with better mechanical integrity than high-temperature-sintered single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
The ZrB2–SiC composite has better oxidation resistance than single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
The ZrB2–SiC composite has better resistance to liquid plating-metal corrosion than single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
SiC particles promote densification of ZrB2.
SiC contributes to formation of a protective silica-based phase during oxidation.
SiC acts as a sintering aid for ZrB2 at temperatures below 1700 °C.
SiC enhances grain-boundary cohesion in ZrB2 at lower sintering temperatures.
High-temperature exposure of the composite forms a protective SiO2-rich layer.
The SiO2-rich layer limits oxygen ingress.
The SiO2-rich layer limits penetration by liquid plating metal.
The composite will have greater mechanical strength and structural integrity than both high-temperature-sintered single-phase ZrB2 and lower-temperature-sintered pure ZrB2.
The composite will exhibit lower oxidation rates than both high-temperature-sintered single-phase ZrB2 and lower-temperature-sintered pure ZrB2.
The intervention is effective at sintering temperatures up to approximately 1700 °C.
The composite remains effective under oxidative service at approximately 1000–1200 °C.
The composite can withstand extended exposure to liquid plating-metal baths.
Performance may degrade under more aggressive or cyclic service environments.

contradictions.description: The claimed baseline and falsification rule require comparison with both high-temperature-sintered single-phase ZrB2 and lower-temperature-sintered pure ZrB2, but the experiment specifies only two groups sintered below 1700 °C. It therefore lacks the high-temperature-sintered single-phase control needed to evaluate the full comparison.
